notes: Curated interview questions, tagged against a CLOSED competency vocabulary. The vocabulary is closed for the same reason rubric_criteria is validated at load: a planner that may invent a competency name produces tags the bank can never match, and the failure is silent. Warmup and closing questions are deliberately absent -- they are structural, identical in every plan, and carry no competency. A question carries BOTH a source (where the text came from, immutable) and a status (whether it may be asked). Generation writes source=generated status=proposed; approval flips the status and never the source, because FR-2 requires a generated question to stay marked as one. `phase_affinity` says which phase of the plan a competency belongs to. It is data rather than logic because the mapping is a judgement someone should be able to read and disagree with, and because the design phase is not scored -- putting a competency there decides that it will be described rather than graded. `min_level` is the least senior candidate a question is fair to ask, junior when omitted. A question is marked mid when it can only be answered from a live system, a team whose decisions you work within, or colleagues' work to review -- experience a junior may simply not have had, so asking it measures their CV rather than how they answer. A junior plan asks one only where nothing fairer fills the slot. Format 2 (1.2): every competency and question names its field, `shared` or one field, and a plan only ever draws on one field's view: its own competencies and questions plus the shared ones. Questions the app generates never live here; they are kept in data/bank_local.json.

competencies.incident_response: diagnosing and resolving production failures, and what changed afterwards
competencies.performance: finding and fixing a scalability or latency problem, with measurement
competencies.data_modelling: schema and data-model change, especially against live data
competencies.system_design: designing a component or service against stated constraints
competencies.testing_quality: deciding something is correct and ready, and how that is known
competencies.collaboration: working through disagreement, feedback and shared decisions
competencies.ownership: supporting what they built after it shipped
competencies.learning: getting productive in an unfamiliar system quickly
competencies.technical_judgement: choosing between options and revisiting the choice later
competencies.prioritisation: choosing what comes first when not everything can be done
competencies.stakeholder_management: keeping the people a piece of work affects informed and on side
competencies.influence: changing a decision or a habit they had no authority over
competencies.decision_making: making a call on incomplete information and owning how it went
competencies.coordination: getting several people's work to land together
competencies.analysis: turning a question into an analysis someone acted on
competencies.data_quality: finding and handling data that was wrong, missing or misleading
competencies.insight_communication: getting a finding understood and used by people who are not analysts
competencies.metric_design: defining a measure so it tracks what matters
competencies.investigation: working an open analytical problem from question to approach
competencies.discovery: finding out what users need before building it
competencies.product_strategy: choosing where a product goes next and getting it agreed
competencies.product_metrics: judging a product by measures chosen in advance
competencies.scope_tradeoffs: cutting or reshaping scope to ship something useful
competencies.product_sense: reasoning through a product problem from user to solution
competencies.user_research: learning first-hand how people behave and what they need
competencies.design_iteration: changing a design on evidence rather than taste
competencies.usability_evaluation: testing whether people can use a design and acting on what failed
competencies.accessibility: making a design work for people with disabilities
competencies.design_handoff: getting a design built as intended
competencies.design_process: working a design problem from brief to a proposal
competencies.planning_scheduling: turning a goal into a schedule people commit to
competencies.risk_management: spotting what could go wrong and acting before it did
competencies.scope_control: handling requests to change what was agreed
competencies.resource_budget: delivering within the people and money a project had
competencies.status_reporting: telling people where a project really stands
competencies.delivery_planning: planning the delivery of a described project from scratch

questions.text: Describe a production incident you were responsible for resolving.
Tell me about a time you found the cause of something only after your first explanation turned out to be wrong.
Describe a failure that reached users before anyone on the team noticed it.
Walk me through a performance or scalability problem you've hit. What did you measure, and what did you change?
Tell me about a time you made something faster and could show by how much.
Describe a time you decided a performance problem was not worth fixing.
Tell me about a schema or data-model change you've made to a system that was already live.
Describe a data model you inherited and had to work against rather than change.
Tell me about a migration or backfill you ran, and how you knew it had worked.
Walk me through how you'd design a rate limiter for a public API. Take a minute first if you want.
How would you design a service that has to keep working when the database it depends on is unavailable? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose you had to move a nightly batch job to run continuously instead. How would you approach it? Take a minute first if you want.
Describe how you decide a change is ready to ship. Use a recent example.
Tell me about a bug that your tests should have caught and didn't.
Describe a time you shipped something deliberately without full test coverage.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision on your team.
Tell me about a time you gave difficult feedback to a colleague.
Describe a decision your team made that you disagreed with and went along with anyway.
Describe how you've handled being on-call, or supporting something you built.
Tell me about something you shipped that didn't work out the way you expected.
Tell me about a piece of work you finished that nobody asked you to do.
Tell me about a time you had to learn an unfamiliar codebase quickly.
Describe something technical you had to learn recently because the work required it.
Tell me about a technical decision you made that you'd make differently now.
Describe a time you chose the slower, more careful approach and had to justify it.
Tell me about a time you removed something rather than adding to it.
Describe a time you helped someone else get unstuck on work that wasn't yours.
Tell me about a review comment you left that changed how someone worked.
Tell me about a time you worked with someone you found difficult.
Describe a time someone gave you feedback you didn't agree with at first.
Tell me about a time you and a colleague wanted to do the same piece of work in different ways.
Describe a mistake you made at work, and what you did about it.
Tell me about a time you took on something outside your usual responsibilities.
Tell me about a commitment you made that you couldn't keep, and how you handled it.
Tell me about a time you had to get up to speed quickly in an area you knew little about.
Describe a skill you taught yourself because your work needed it.
Tell me about a piece of feedback that changed how you work.
Describe a time you explained something difficult to a colleague so they could do it on their own.
Tell me about someone you supported over several weeks, and what changed for them.
Tell me about a time you handed someone a task you could have done faster yourself.
Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline.
Describe a time you said no to a request, or pushed it back, so something more important got done.
Tell me about a time your priorities changed suddenly part-way through a piece of work.
Tell me about a time two people you were working for wanted different things from you.
Describe a time you had to tell someone outside your team news they didn't want to hear.
Tell me about a time you kept people outside your team up to date on work that affected them.
Describe a time you changed how something was done at work.
Tell me about a time you changed someone's mind about a decision that wasn't yours to make.
Tell me about a time you tried to persuade someone and didn't succeed.
Tell me about a decision you made without all the information you wanted.
Describe a decision you made that turned out to be wrong, and what you did when you found out.
Tell me about a time you had to choose between two reasonable options. How did you decide?
Tell me about a time you had to get several people's work to come together by a deadline.
Describe a time a hand-off between you and someone else went wrong.
Tell me about a time you depended on another team to get your work done.
Tell me about an analysis you did that changed a decision someone was about to make.
Walk me through an analysis where the first answer you found turned out to be wrong.
Tell me about a time you were given a vague question and had to work out what was really being asked.
Walk me through an experiment or A/B test you analysed, and what you concluded.
Describe a time the data you were given turned out to be wrong or incomplete.
Tell me how you checked that a dataset was fit to use before relying on it. Use a recent example.
Tell me about a time you found a problem in data that other people were already using.
Tell me about a time you explained a finding to people without a data background.
Describe a time someone misread or misused a number or chart you'd produced. What did you do?
Tell me about a recommendation you made from data that people pushed back on.
Tell me about a dashboard or report you built. How did you know people used it?
Tell me about a metric you defined or changed. How did you make sure it measured the right thing?
Describe a time a number was improving while the thing it was meant to track was getting worse.
Suppose weekly sign-ups dropped by twenty per cent last week and nobody knows why. How would you find out? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose a team wants to know whether a new feature made customers spend more. How would you work that out? Take a minute first if you want.
How would you measure customer satisfaction for a delivery service using only the data it already collects? Take a minute first if you want.
Walk me through how customer research changed a product decision you'd made.
Describe how you found out whether a problem was worth solving before a team started building.
Tell me about a time what users asked for and what they needed turned out to be different.
Tell me about a time two stakeholders wanted different things from your roadmap.
Tell me about a product direction you set or changed, and how you got others behind it.
Tell me about a product bet you made that didn't pay off.
Tell me about a metric you set for a product, and how it moved.
Describe a launch that didn't go the way you planned.
Tell me about a time you stopped or rolled back something because of what the data showed.
Tell me about a feature you decided not to build, and how you made that call.
Tell me about a time you cut scope to hit a date. How did you decide what to cut?
Describe a time engineers told you something would take far longer than you expected. What did you do?
Suppose you run the app a public library uses for borrowing, and loans have fallen this year. What would you look at, and what might you build? Take a minute first if you want.
How would you decide what to build first in a new app that helps housemates split bills? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose a few loud customers keep asking for a feature most customers would never use. How would you decide whether to build it? Take a minute first if you want.
Tell me about a piece of research you ran that changed a design's direction.
Describe a time what users said and what they did turned out to be different.
Tell me about a project where you had very little user research to work from.
Tell me about a design decision you changed after usability testing.
Describe a time a design tested well but caused problems once people used it for real.
Tell me about a design you reworked substantially because of feedback. What changed, and why?
Describe a time you had to let go of a design you liked.
Describe a time you had to defend a design to a stakeholder who disagreed.
Walk me through how you made something you designed more accessible.
Describe a time you argued for an accessibility fix that others saw as optional.
Tell me about a time an engineering constraint forced you to change a design.
Tell me about a design that was built differently from how you designed it. What happened?
Describe how you worked with engineers to get a tricky interaction built the way you intended.
Suppose a council wants residents to report potholes from their phones. How would you approach designing that? Take a minute first if you want.
How would you approach redesigning a checkout that many customers abandon at the payment step? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose you had one week to improve an internal form that staff complain about. How would you spend it? Take a minute first if you want.
Tell me about a project plan you put together. How did you work out the schedule?
Tell me about a project that was slipping, and how you brought it back.
Tell me about a deadline you thought was unrealistic. What did you do about it?
Describe how you got people who didn't report to you to deliver on time.
Tell me about a risk you spotted early, and what you did about it.
Describe a risk you missed. What happened, and what do you do differently now?
Tell me about a time you had to decide whether to escalate a problem or handle it yourself.
Describe a time you had to manage scope creep.
Tell me about a time someone asked to add work to a project part-way through. How did you handle it?
Tell me about a project where you had to work within a tight budget or headcount.
Describe a time you lost a key person part-way through a project. What did you do?
Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a sponsor or client.
Tell me about a time a status report you wrote turned out to be too optimistic.
Suppose you're asked to move a forty-person office to a new building in three months without disrupting work. How would you plan it? Take a minute first if you want.
How would you plan the rollout of a new booking system to five clinics, when one of them is much busier than the rest? Take a minute first if you want.
Suppose you've just taken over a project that is six weeks late, and the sponsor wants a new date by Friday. How would you approach it? Take a minute first if you want.
